messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 23
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Urban Planner
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 77

He still walks the same route home from the office most evenings, even though he knows it is the street where it happened. The route is shorter, he tells himself, and it saves time. But the truth is that he walks it because he is testing something—a kind of private ritual he cannot explain. He watches the streetlights, counts the steps between the bus stop and the corner where the shadows pool. He checks for broken glass, for the shape of a person leaning too long against a wall. Two blocks from his apartment, he stops. His heart is already beating too fast. He tells himself to breathe. He does not know why he keeps doing this.

The assault happened seven months ago. He was coming home late from a community planning meeting, a binder of zoning proposals tucked under his arm. It was just after eleven, a mild Tuesday. He remembers the sound of his own footsteps, the weight of his laptop bag. Two men came from behind the dumpster near the abandoned convenience store—the one he had flagged for redevelopment in his last report. He does not remember their faces, only the pressure: a hand over his mouth, a knee in his back, the strap of his bag pulled so hard it cut into his collarbone. They took his wallet, his phone, the binder. One of them kicked him twice in the ribs after he was already on the ground. Then they were gone. He lay there for three minutes, maybe four, before a woman walking her dog found him.

At the hospital, he gave the police a statement. He said he could not identify anyone. He did not want to look at photos. The attending nurse gave him a card for a therapist. He put it in his jacket pocket and forgot about it. The next day he went back to work. His supervisor asked if he needed time off. He said he was fine.

He is not fine. He knows this now, although he has not said it aloud to anyone. He works in the urban planning department for a mid-sized city, and his job requires him to think about public space—parks, sidewalks, transit hubs, lighting. He used to love walking through neighborhoods, sketching ideas, imagining how a bench or a bike lane could transform a corner. Now he cannot step into a public square without scanning the exits. At staff meetings, when the team discusses new nightlife zones or extended transit hours, he feels his chest tighten. He has started recommending more lighting in his project proposals, more cameras, more harsh, overlapping visibility. His colleagues call him thorough. He does not correct them.

He has stopped going out after dark entirely. He tells his friends he is busy with work, which is true, but it is also not the whole truth. He has not been to a bar or a restaurant in months. His mother calls from home—home, the country he left three years ago—and he tells her everything is good, that he is working hard, that he is happy. He hears his own voice go flat. After the call, he sits in the dark of his apartment and feels nothing, which is worse than feeling sad.

At night, he sleeps in fits. He has a recurring dream: he is walking the same street, but the streetlights are off, and the shadows are moving. He wakes with his heart pounding, his hands gripping the sheets. Sometimes he checks his front door three times before he can breathe again. Once, last month, he got in his car and drove around the block for an hour, convinced someone was following him. He knew it was irrational. He could not stop.

His mind replays the assault in fragments: the pressure on his ribs, the smell of damp concrete, the sound of the bag strap breaking. He does not think about the assault in the daytime—he has trained himself not to. But at three in the morning, lying in the dark, he sees it in perfect detail. He feels the shame of lying on the ground, of not fighting back.

At work this week, his supervisor asked him to lead a community engagement session for a proposed park redesign in a neighborhood similar to the one where he was attacked. He said yes immediately, the way he says yes to everything now. The meeting is in two days. He has already mapped the room, located the exits, planned his route to the parking lot. He knows it will be fine. He will survive it. But he does not know how to tell anyone that surviving it is not the same as living through it.
